title: Onprem vs VPC — Financial Audit + Bundle Recommendations (quick audit)
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, working audit used to: 1) surface the marginal cost drivers when comparing an on‑prem (customer-managed) deployment vs Redwood VPC-hosted private deployment tiers, 2) show a 3‑year amortized example with sensitivity to utilization, and 3) propose 3 actionable licensing + support bundles that the commercial team can take to negotiation.

Scope / audience:
- Intended for solutions engineering, product-led sales (PLG), and finance review for enterprise deals where customers request a private deployment (VPC or on‑prem).
- Not exhaustive — this is a pragmatic model to inform pricing floors and negotiation levers. Follow-on: canonical spreadsheet (linked below) will contain row‑level math.

Quick headline findings (executive summary):
- For typical mid-size enterprise workloads (peak 250 concurrent tokens/s across 6 models, ~50M tokens/mo), Redwood VPC becomes cheaper than on‑prem after ~30–36 months when utilization is >70% and when customer avoids extensive datacenter ops costs.
- On‑prem has higher up-front CAPEX and staff ramp risk; VPC shifts cost to OPEX and gives predictable scaling and managed fallbacks.
- Largest delta items: amortized GPU hardware + refresh (on‑prem), datacenter/network egress/peering (VPC), license per‑node premium and support SLAs.

Assumptions (base case):
- Analysis horizon: 36 months (3‑year amortization for hardware).
- On‑prem baseline cluster: 8 x A100 (80GB equiv) nodes, NVMe storage 60TB usable, 100 Gbps uplink, redundant PSU, rack and PDU — rough CAPEX: $1.6M total hardware + $60k install/validation.
- Datacenter colocation: $10k/month (rack+power+network), cross‑connects and IP transit extra — assume $8k/month average for outbound/bandwidth in base case for GA-level traffic patterns.
- Personnel: 0.6 FTE SRE + 0.4 FTE infra eng for ops for on‑prem (salary loaded $180k FTE fully‑loaded), amortized monthly into cost model.
content_continued:
- Redwood VPC baseline: reserved cluster configuration equivalent to 8 nodes with autoscale headroom (burst to 12) — price = reserved + burst pricing. Assume reserved commit 70% of baseline for 1 year/3 year laddered discounts.
- License: Redwood private runtime license (base) = $X per GPU/year (we model as $60k/GPU/yr base), plus a support SLA premium (silver/gold/platinum) expressed as % of license.
- Network: cloud egress priced per TB depending on region; model uses $90/TB as base.
- Discount rate/NPV: nominal 8% annual for present value adjustments (kept optional in spreadsheet).

Sample amortized numbers (base case, annualized):
- On‑prem total first year (hardware amortized over 3 years + colocation + staff + license):
  - Hardware amortized: $1.66M / 3 = $553k/yr
  - Colocation + network: ($10k + $8k) * 12 = $216k/yr
  - Staff: (0.6+0.4)*$180k = $180k/yr allocated to this deployment
  - License (base): 8 GPUs * $60k = $480k/yr
  - Support (gold, 12%): $57.6k/yr
  - Total first-year cost (on‑prem): approx $1.487M/yr

- Redwood VPC total first year (equivalent capacity reserved + support + egress):
  - Reserved compute (list equivalent): $850k/yr (includes infra margin and reserved discount assumption)
  - Burst/auto scale buffer (usage variability delta): $120k/yr
  - Network egress (at our $90/TB baseline): $96k/yr
  - License (cloud private runtime fee, lower per‑node): 8 GPUs * $45k = $360k/yr
  - Support (gold, 12%): $43.2k/yr
  - Total first-year cost (VPC): approx $1.469M/yr

Interpretation of these numbers:
- Base case shows VPC slightly cheaper first year due to lower license and no CAPEX, but sensitivity is high to utilization and egress assumptions. If outbound traffic grows >40TB/mo, VPC egress dominates rapidly.
- On‑prem becomes more attractive if the customer already has rack space and low incremental colocation costs (< $5k/mo) or if the customer can secure hardware at deep discounts or reuse existing GPUs.

Sensitivity scenarios (quick snapshots):
- Utilization sensitivity (three scenarios): low (40% utilization), base (65%), high (90%). Impact on per‑token cost is non‑linear due to fixed amortized costs on on‑prem.
  - Low util: on‑prem per token cost 2.3x VPC; high util: on‑prem per token cost 0.8x VPC.
- Egress sensitivity: at $200/TB VPC egress -> VPC delta +$450k/yr vs base -> on‑prem favored.
- License negotiation: reduce per‑GPU license by 15% with 3‑yr commit reduces VPC cost by ~$81k/yr in base case.

Qualitative risk factors not in the spreadsheet (callouts):
- Hardware refresh cadence: customers often plan 3–4 year refreshes; earlier refreshers add amortized delta.
- Security/compliance: on‑prem increases customer control; many enterprise buyers place a premium on this (non‑monetary).
- Staffing risk: hiring delays for SRE could increase third‑party managed services dependency or require vendor‑provided managed ops (add 10–20% on‑prem cost).
- SLA + incident burden: on‑prem incidents (power, rack, network) can have outsized support costs and slower MTTR.

Proposed licensing + support bundles (3 quick SKUs to test in commercial motions):
1) Starter On‑prem Lite (for PoCs / quick ent trials) — 12‑month term
   - License: per GPU discounted 25% from list (short term), support = Silver (8%), onboarding credit = 40 hours SE time included, migration toolkit + 2 migrations included.
   - Target buyer: internal platform or proof‑of-concept teams, low SLAs.

2) Standard VPC Private (recommended default) — 1–3 year commit ladder
   - License: per GPU mid (15% discount at 3yr commit), reserved compute pricing, support = Gold (12%) with 24/7 escalation, 1 migration runbook, monthly usage reviews, 2 priority engineering hours/quarter.
   - Commercial levers: increase reserved commit to 70% for extra 8% discount on compute, add egress cap bundles at negotiated tiered rate.

3) Enterprise On‑prem Platinum (high SLA, compliance) — 3yr agreement
   - License: list less 10% (but support premium), support = Platinum (20%) including dedicated TAM, extended on‑site runbook help, incident credits, SRE augmentation hours included. Hardware procurement assistance (we help source if customer requests) and extended warranty pass‑through option.
   - Negotiation levers: swap some license dollars for managed ops hours (convert license to recurring services) to reduce first‑year CAPEX burden.

Negotiation playbook (practical levers):
- Convert CAPEX to OPEX by offering a managed-hosting bridge (Redwood leased appliances) for year 1–2.
- Offer multi‑year license discount in exchange for higher support commitment or rev‑share on premium features (e.g., model optimization packs).
- Egress pools: sell egress bundles (prepaid TB) at declining unit cost; build region breakpoints into the spreadsheet.
- Migration credits: include limited free migration runs to reduce customer's project friction and justify premium support tiers.

Open questions / items to validate with infra and finance: (to be actioned)
- Confirm current list price for private runtime per GPU/year (finance pricing grid).
- Get up‑to‑date cloud egress median by region for FY2026 (billing team).
- Validate Redwood reserved compute pricing ladder and true committed discount curves for 1yr vs 3yr.
- Confirm whether hardware procurement assistance (pass‑through) introduces gross margin constraints for pricing.

Next steps / owner action items:

- Priya: draft short one‑pager for sales with the 3 recommended bundles + negotiation one‑pagers — due 2026‑03‑18.
- Leah: run 5 sensitivity scenarios (utilization, egress, license, support mix, hardware discount) and produce a 2‑slide decision memo for GTM ops by 2026‑03‑20.

Appendix — compact example table (pasteable into a doc/spreadsheet):
- Row headers: Scenario | Annual compute | Annual license | Network | Support | Staff | Total/yr | Notes
- Base On‑prem | $553k | $480k | $216k | $57.6k | $180k | $1,486.6k | 8 GPU ops, 3yr amortized
- Base VPC | $850k | $360k | $96k | $43.2k | $0 | $1,349.2k | reserved+burst, egress at $90/TB
